properties.description: Sisters (released 2018) is a comedy-drama starring Lucy Durack, Antonia Prebble and Maria Angelico that follows three women who discover they are biological sisters after uncovering that their father used his own sperm in IVF procedures. The series combines dark, often deadpan humor with earnest, character-driven drama as it tracks Julia, Roxy and Edie through the emotional fallout and shifting family bonds. It explores themes of identity, belonging and medical ethics while maintaining a warm, bittersweet tone. The show foregrounds intimate performances and observational visuals to balance humor and pathos.
properties.plot_summary: Three women from different walks of life discover they are biological sisters after one of them learns their Nobel-Prize-winning father secretly used his own sperm in multiple IVF procedures. The revelation — and the possibility of hundreds of half-siblings — forces them to re-evaluate identity, family bonds and trust. The series follows Julia, an amiable but aimless woman who uncovers the truth, Roxy, a children's TV presenter struggling with pills, and Edie, an uptight lawyer dealing with personal upheaval. It balances darkly comic moments with heartfelt, character-driven drama as the trio navigate surprising connections and emotional fallout.
properties.audience_identity: People who appreciate empathetic, character-driven stories with darkly comic edges—often curious about family dynamics, identity questions and ethical dilemmas, and who value nuanced performances over plot spectacle.
properties.genre_description: A character-focused comedy-drama that blends intimate, naturalistic storytelling with dry, dark humor to examine interpersonal dynamics and moral tensions within a contemporary family setting.
properties.style_description: Naturalistic and intimate, the series uses warm, observational cinematography and deadpan comedic timing to foreground character moments and emotional nuance.

properties.description: The Split (2018), directed in part by Jessica Hobbs, is a British legal-family drama led by Nicola Walker as the central divorce lawyer, with Stephen Mangan among the principal cast. Set in London’s family-law scene, the series follows a woman torn between a prestigious firm and the rival practice run by her own family as she handles high-stakes divorces, custody disputes, and ethically fraught client work. Grounded in intimate character study, the show explores themes of familial loyalty, professional rivalry, love and betrayal, and personal growth through a palette of realistic legal procedure and emotionally resonant family storytelling. Its tone is serious and nuanced, combining courtroom tension with domestic drama and placing moral ambiguity and relational complexity at the heart of its narrative.
properties.plot_summary: A family of high-powered divorce lawyers navigate the emotional and procedural complexities of marital breakdowns while their own relationships fray under pressure. The central figure is a driven divorce lawyer who splits her time between a prominent London practice and the private turmoil of her family’s rival firm. Cases range from delicate negotiations and custody battles to acrimonious courtroom showdowns, each illuminating the personal histories, secrets, and loyalties that bind and break the family. Professional rivalries, ethical dilemmas, and overlapping client conflicts force the characters to confront compromises between career ambition and private life, and to reckon with past choices that shape both their marriages and their legal strategies.

properties.style_description: Visuals and direction favor a restrained, polished realism: understated cinematography, naturalistic lighting, and close, intimate framing to capture subtle emotional shifts. properties.description: I'm Sorry (2017) is a single-camera comedy series starring Andrea Savage, with Tom Everett Scott and Olive Petrucci among the main cast, that aired on TruTV. The show follows a seemingly confident comedy writer and mother whose attempts to do the right thing repeatedly yield socially awkward, cringe-filled situations. Blending dark, observational humor with genuine warmth, it explores parenting, marriage, and social anxiety through character-driven episodes. The tone mixes sharp, adult-centered satire with tenderness toward its flawed characters.
properties.plot_summary: A seemingly confident comedy writer, wife, and mother struggles to reconcile her public persona with private insecurities, repeatedly landing in socially awkward and embarrassing situations. Episodes mine everyday domestic moments for cringe and unexpected humor as her attempts at being virtuous or politically correct often backfire. The series balances sharp, adult-centered satire with genuine warmth, exploring the tender realities of parenting and marriage beneath the laughs.

properties.description: Here and Now (2018), created by Alan Ball and starring Tim Robbins, Holly Hunter, and Daniel Zovatto, is a dark comedy-drama that follows a progressive Portland family as personal crises expose cultural and psychological fault lines. Across ten episodes the show blends realistic, character-driven drama with occasional fantastical visions to interrogate adoption, race, mental illness, and spirituality. Ball’s tone is simultaneously empathetic and unsettling, using quiet, observational direction and surreal beats to provoke reflection. The series aims for a contemplative emotional register rather than quick resolutions.
properties.plot_summary: A progressive Portland family raising four children — three adopted from abroad and one biological daughter — confronts crises that strain their ideals, relationships, and sanity. As members face addiction, cultural conflict, grief, and unexplained visions, long-held assumptions about identity and parenthood unravel. The series alternates between dry humor and unsettling, sometimes fantastical episodes that test empathy and belief. Through intimate character work it examines how personal and political pressures collide in contemporary America.

properties.description: Rake (2011) is an Australian comedy-drama starring Richard Roxburgh, with supporting performances from Matt Day and Kate Box; writers on the series include Peter Duncan, Andrew Knight and Charles Waterstreet. It follows a brilliant but self-destructive criminal lawyer who repeatedly wins improbable cases while his personal life — marked by addiction, gambling debt and fraught relationships — spirals. Tonally the series mixes dark satire, courtroom drama and seedy, character-driven comedy to probe questions of justice, corruption and personal morality. The result is often uproarious, frequently uncomfortable, and anchored by a charismatic antihero performance.
properties.plot_summary: A brilliant but self-destructive criminal lawyer repeatedly wins apparently unwinnable cases while his private life unravels: addiction, massive gambling debt and chaotic relationships. He navigates Sydney’s courts and seedy underworld with sharp wit and moral flexibility, often creating as many problems as he solves. Episodes blend courtroom battles with dark, satirical set pieces that expose corruption, politics and personal compromise.
